Em = g'K+ (Ek) + g'Na+ (ENa) + g'Ca2+ (ECa) -----------------------  This equation describes how the membrane potential is determined by the equilibrium potentials for each ion and the relative membrane conductance for that ion.  g' = slope of the I-V curve for a particular ion  gH = membrane conductance for H+   gK+ = membrane conductance for K+  gNa+ = membrane conductance for Na+  gCa2+ = membrane conductance for Ca2+  Ek = equilibrium potential for K+  ENa = equilibrium potential for Na+  ECa = equilibrium potential for Ca2+  Note: g' is sometimes called the maximum conductance for that ion. It is the maximal conductance that could be achieved if no other ion channels were open.  For example, if only Na+ channels were open then g'Na+ would be the conductance.  However, this is not always true as more than one type of ion channel may be open at once and therefore g' is the slope of the I-V curve and not necessarily equal to the conductance of the open ion channels.  You can use this equation to work out the relative proportions of different ion channels contributing to the membrane conductance.  g'K+ /g'Na+ will give you the proportion of K+ channels present in the membrane compared to Na+ channels.  g'Na+ /g'Ca2+ will give you the proportion of Na+ channels present in the membrane compared to Ca2+ channels.  g'Ca2+ /g'K+ will give you the proportion of Ca2+ channels present in the membrane compared to K+ channels.  e.g. If g'K+ = 10 mS/cm2 and g'Na+ = 50 mS/cm2 then the ratio of K+ to Na+ channels is 1:5 or 20% K+ to 80% Na+ channels are present in the membrane. 25/8 is the only figure which has a mean greater than 120 and a pulsatility index less than 30. Therefore it must be PA pressure. All other figures are systemic pressures. 120/70 - mean 120, pulsatility index 160/80 - mean 135, pulsatility index 30 50/23 - mean 40, pulsatility index 1890/44 - mean 51, pulsatility index 2725/8 - mean 17, pulsatility index 6  Note that the pulsatility index is calculated by taking the difference between systolic and diastolic pressures. So for example, 140-80 = 60, then 60/8 = 7.5. This gives us a pulsatility index of 7.5. We know that the normal range for PA pressure in adults is 20-30. Therefore as we have a value outside this range, we can rule out any of the other answers. Also, remember that PA pressures should always be lower than systemic pressures.  Hope this helps! 1st line of treatment: Reperfusion therapy - re-opening of the vessel with PCI/thrombolysis (clot busting drug). If this isn't possible then stabilisation of the patient with morphine, oxygen, nitrates and aspirin. The others are all important but come later in management. Treatment of an MI is one of the most common SBA questions on the case 5 exam. A great way to remember it is MOANA. MorphineOxygen Aspirin Nitrates Aspirin A = ACE inhibitors (blood pressure lowering) Note: Beta blockers are also used for blood pressure control but not in the initial stages of an MI. PCI is percutaneous coronary intervention - inserting a stent into the artery to open it up which is another option of reperfusion therapy. Thrombolytics are clot busting drugs that can be used to treat MI if PCI or stents aren't available. Defibrillation would be used to treat ventricular fibrillation. This is where there is chaotic electrical activity in the heart leading to no output from the ventricles.  1st step is to try to restore a normal rhythm with synchronised cardioversion (electric shock) and then give drugs such as adrenaline and lidocaine to stop the arrhythmia occurring again. Vitamin A (retinol) is essential for growth and development. It is also needed for healthy skin, eyesight and immunity. Vitamin A deficiency can cause night blindness and can lead to permanent damage to the retina. In children, vitamin A deficiency can cause growth retardation and increased susceptibility to infections. Source - http://www.nhs.uk/Conditions/vitamins-minerals/Pages/Vitamin-A.aspx  Also, Vitamin A is fat soluble and therefore it can be stored in the body. This means that if someone does not get enough vitamin A from their diet they will use up the stores in their bodies before showing any signs of deficiency. A 12 year old child would have used up all the vitamin A reserves in their body, which explains why he is small for his age (stunted growth).  Other symptoms of vitamin A include:- poor vision; dry eyes; excessive tearing; red swollen eyes; inflamed mucous membranes in the nose, mouth and throat; thickened hair and dandruff; and cracked lips.  Vitamin A deficiency is common in developing countries. It is rare in the UK, although it can occur in people who do not eat meat or drink full-fat milk. C is the correct answer! The radial nerve innervates the extensor muscles of the wrist and hand. This means that if it is damaged, the patient will not be able to extend their wrist and fingers. 100mg/day is the RDA for tryptophan. Low levels of this amino acid leads to depleted serotonin synthesis. Serotonin is a monoamine neurotransmitter that has antidepressant effects. Tryptophan competes with large neutral amino acids (leucine, isoleucine etc) for entry into the blood stream across the intestinal wall. When there is an increase in the amount of these other amino acids, tryptophan uptake is reduced and therefore it's levels are lowered. Whole milk has a high protein content so would have a higher concentration of these competing amino acids than skimmed milk - hence it is important to drink skimmed milk if you want to ensure you get adequate tryptophan from your diet. Influenza is caused by an infection with an influenza virus. There are three main types of influenza viruses; influenza A, B and C. These differ in their antigenicity (how easily the immune system recognises them) and pathogenicity (the ability to cause disease). Type A viruses are the most variable and cause severe epidemics and pandemics (worldwide outbreaks of infectious disease). Type B viruses are less variable and tend to cause milder infections than type A. Type C viruses are uncommon and only cause mild respiratory infections. All three types of influenza viruses are enveloped single stranded RNA viruses belonging to the family Orthomyxoviridae. They all contain eight structural proteins; hemagglutinin (HA), neuraminidase (NA), matrix protein 1 and 2 (M1 and M2), acidic polymerase, nucleoprotein and two ion channels. Virus entry into cells is mediated by HA binding to sialic acid receptors on the surface of cells. The virus then fuses with the cell membrane and releases its genetic material into the cytoplasm of the cell. Once inside the cell, the viral RNA is transcribed into viral mRNA and then translated into new viral proteins. Influenza can lead to complications such as pneumonia, bronchitis and otitis media (inflammation of the middle ear). It can even be fatal. Saturated fatty acids are fatty acids that contain no double carbon-carbon bonds and therefore only single bonds between carbons. Unsaturated fatty acids are fatty acids that have one or more double carbon-carbon bonds and therefore also have single bonds between carbons. Cis fats are unsaturated fatty acids in which the hydrogen atoms attached to the carbons on either side of the double bond are located on the same side as each other. Trans fats are unsaturated fatty acids in which the hydrogen atoms attached to the carbons on either side of the double bond are located on opposite sides of each other. Monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs) are unsaturated fatty acids that have one double bond. Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) are unsaturated fatty acids that have two or more double bonds. Omega-3 fatty acids are polyunsaturated fatty acids that have their first double bond three carbons from the end of the chain. Omega-6 fatty acids are polyunsaturated fatty acids that have their first double bond six carbons from the end of the chain. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fatty_acid#Saturated_fatty_acids https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fatty_acid#Unsaturated_fatty_acids https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cis%E2%80%93trans_isomerism https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trans_fat https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monounsaturated_fat https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyunsaturated_fat https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omega-3_fatty_acid https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omega-6_fatty_acid

The superficial fibular nerve innervates the extensor digitorum brevis muscle which is responsible for extension at the metatarsophalangeal joints and interphalangeal joints of the 4th and 5th digits. It also provides motor innervation to the anterior tibial muscle. Loss of sensation in the lateral side of the 5th digit indicates that this nerve has been damaged. Also, the inability to everte the foot points towards injury to the superficial fibular nerve because the tibialis anterior muscle is supplied by this nerve. The deep fibular nerve innervates the extensor digitorum longus muscle which extends the digits at the metatarsophalangeal joints and interphalangeal joints of 2nd, 3rd and 4th digits. Injury to this nerve would cause loss of extension at these joints. The medial plantar nerve supplies the abductor hallucis muscle and the flexor hallucis longus muscle. Damage to this nerve causes loss of function in these two muscles which will result in inability to abduct the big toe and flex it at the interphalangeal joint. The saphenous nerve is a continuation of the tibial nerve and its function is not directly related to the symptoms shown by this patient. The lateral plantar nerve innervates the lateral side of the 4th and 5th digits and the small muscles of the arch of the foot. Damage to this nerve results in loss of sensation on the lateral side of the 4th and 5th digits as well as numbness over the arch of the foot. However, this patient still has sensation over the dorsum of his foot except for the areas mentioned above. This rules out damage to the lateral plantar nerve. Therefore the superficial fibular nerve is the only option that fits all the criteria. Source: Neuroscience Case 10, Dr Watson's "Case 7", Dr Watson's "Case 8" and Dr Watson's "Case 9" lectures. Haemophilia A is a disease caused by a deficiency of clotting factor VIII (8). It is inherited in an X-linked recessive manner and affects only males. Haemophiliacs may experience spontaneous bleeding as well as excessive bleeding following injuries or surgery. It is a relatively rare condition, occurring in about 1 in 5000 male births. Symptoms are often first noticed at an early age, between 2 and 6 years old, although the severity of symptoms varies greatly among affected individuals. Haemophilia A is usually diagnosed with the help of blood tests that check the activity of factor VIII in the blood. Treatment involves replacing factor VIII, either by injection or by infusion. People with haemophilia A have an increased risk of liver disease due to the use of clotting factor concentrates. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haemophilia_A   Haemophilia B is a disease caused by a deficiency of clotting factor IX (9). It is inherited in an X-linked recessive manner and affects both males and females, but is most severe in males. Haemophiliacs may experience spontaneous bleeding as well as excessive bleeding following injuries or surgery. It is a relatively rare condition, occurring in about 1 in 30,000 live births. Symptoms are often first noticed at an early age, between 2 and 4 years old, although the severity of symptoms varies greatly among affected individuals. Haemophilia B is usually diagnosed with the help of blood tests that check the activity of factor IX in the blood. Treatment involves replacing factor IX, either by injection or by infusion. People with haemophilia B have an increased risk of liver disease due to the use of clotting factor concentrates. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haemophilia_B Haemophilia C is a disease caused by a deficiency of clotting factor XI (11). It is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner and affects both males and females, but is most severe in males. Cortical reaction - release of cortical enzymes that break down the zona pellucida and allow sperm entry into the egg.  Acrosome Reaction - occurs when the acrosome comes into contact with the membrane of the egg. It releases enzymes to digest the cumulus cells so that the sperm can penetrate through the zona pellucida.  Spermiogenesis - the process of sperm maturation.
